title: Medical-Surgical Nursing I
description: Fluid and electrolyte care, peri-operative nursing, wound care, and the nursing management of respiratory and cardiovascular conditions.

topics.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid–Base Nursing
topics.summary: Assessing hydration, IV fluid therapy, fluid balance charting and electrolyte imbalances.

notes.b: Dehydration signs: thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) and concentrated urine. Fluid overload signs: oedema, raised JVP, breathlessness, basal crackles, weight gain. An accurate fluid balance (intake–output) chart and daily weights guide therapy. Crystalloids: 0.9% sodium chloride (isotonic, resuscitation), Ringer's lactate/Hartmann's (balanced), 5% dextrose (effectively free water — not for resuscitation), dextrose–saline. Colloids expand plasma volume. Nurses check the prescription, fluid, rate, cannula site (phlebitis: redness, pain, swelling — remove cannula) and watch for infiltration and overload. Drip rate (drops/min) = volume (mL) × drop factor ÷ time (min).
k: Dehydration: dry mucosa, poor turgor, low urine

notes.b: Normal values: sodium 135–145 mmol/L; potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L; calcium 2.2–2.6 mmol/L. Hypokalaemia (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea) causes muscle weakness, ileus and arrhythmias (flat T waves, U waves). Hyperkalaemia (renal failure, excess supplements, haemolysed sample) causes peaked T waves and cardiac arrest risk. IV potassium must never be given as a bolus; it must be diluted and infused slowly (usually ≤ 10 mmol/h peripherally) with cardiac monitoring for high rates. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion and seizures; rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
k: Never give IV potassium as a bolus

topics.title: Peri-operative Nursing
topics.summary: Pre-operative preparation, intra-operative safety and post-operative care and complications.

notes.b: Pre-operative preparation: informed consent (obtained by the surgeon), identification band, allergy check, baseline vital signs and investigations, fasting (commonly no solids for 6 hours and clear fluids up to 2 hours before anaesthesia, per local policy), skin preparation, removal of jewellery, dentures and nail polish, bladder emptying, pre-medication as prescribed, thromboprophylaxis (stockings, early mobilisation, heparin) and psychological preparation. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign in, time out, sign out) prevents wrong-site surgery and retained instruments; swab and instrument counts are performed.
k: Fasting: solids 6 h, clear fluids 2 h
WHO checklist: sign in, time out, sign out

notes.b: In the recovery room, maintain the airway (the commonest early risk — tongue falling back, laryngospasm), monitor vital signs, oxygen saturation, level of consciousness, pain, wound drainage and urine output. Complications: primary haemorrhage (during surgery), reactionary haemorrhage (within 24 hours as BP rises or a ligature slips), secondary haemorrhage (7–10 days, from infection); atelectasis (early post-operative fever, first 48 hours — prevented by deep breathing and early mobilisation); wound infection (day 3–7); deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; urinary retention; paralytic ileus; post-operative nausea and vomiting. Early mobilisation, adequate analgesia and deep-breathing exercises prevent many complications.
k: Early mobilisation prevents DVT and chest infection

topics.title: Wound Care and Infection Prevention in Surgery
topics.summary: Wound healing, types of wounds and dressings, surgical site infection and pressure ulcers.

notes.b: Wound healing phases: haemostasis, inflammation (days 0–4), proliferation (granulation tissue, angiogenesis, epithelialisation — days 4–21) and maturation/remodelling (up to 1–2 years). Healing by primary intention: clean wound edges brought together (sutured surgical wound) — minimal scarring. Secondary intention: wound left open to granulate (infected or large tissue loss) — more scarring. Tertiary (delayed primary) intention: closure after a delay once infection is controlled. Factors delaying healing: infection, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, smoking, steroids, anaemia, old age, poor blood supply and pressure.

Aseptic (non-touch) technique is used for dressings. Normal saline is a safe cleansing solution. Choose dressings to keep a moist wound environment, absorb exudate and protect: films (superficial), hydrocolloids, hydrogels (dry necrotic wounds), alginates and foams (heavy exudate). Surgical site infection signs: redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus, fever and wound breakdown, usually 3–7 days after surgery; take a swab for culture. Wound dehiscence (separation of layers) and evisceration are emergencies — cover with sterile moist saline dressings and call the surgeon. Pressure ulcers are staged 1 (non-blanching erythema) to 4 (full-thickness loss exposing bone/tendon).
k: Dehiscence: cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing

topics.title: Nursing Care of Respiratory Conditions
topics.summary: Oxygen therapy, asthma, pneumonia, tuberculosis and chest drain care.

notes.b: Oxygen is a drug and must be prescribed with target saturations: usually 94–98%, or 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD). Delivery: nasal cannula (1–4 L/min, ~24–40%), simple face mask (5–10 L/min), Venturi mask (fixed, precise concentrations — preferred in COPD), non-rebreather mask with reservoir (10–15 L/min, up to ~85–90%). Position breathless patients upright (high Fowler's). Humidify high-flow oxygen. Observe for fire risk — no smoking or naked flames. Suctioning should be brief (≤ 10–15 seconds) with pre-oxygenation.

Asthma: teach correct inhaler technique (spacer use), recognise severe attack (inability to complete sentences, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest = life-threatening), give nebulised salbutamol and oxygen as prescribed. Pneumonia: monitor vital signs, oxygen, fluids, antibiotics, chest physiotherapy, positioning. Tuberculosis: DOTS (directly observed treatment, short-course), airborne precautions until non-infectious (usually after about 2 weeks of effective treatment), adherence counselling, nutrition, contact tracing, and HIV testing. Underwater-seal chest drain care: keep the drainage bottle below chest level, check swinging (oscillation) and bubbling, never clamp routinely, keep the tubing secure.
k: TB: DOTS, airborne precautions, contact tracing
Chest drain bottle below chest level

topics.title: Nursing Care of Cardiovascular Conditions
topics.summary: Hypertension, heart failure, myocardial infarction, anticoagulant therapy and shock.

notes.b: Hypertension is common in Nigeria and often asymptomatic. Nursing care: accurate BP measurement (correct cuff size, seated rest for 5 minutes, arm at heart level), lifestyle education (salt reduction, weight loss, exercise, limiting alcohol, stopping smoking), and adherence to antihypertensives. Heart failure: monitor daily weight (gain of > 2 kg in 3 days suggests fluid retention), fluid balance, oedema and breathlessness; position upright; restrict salt and sometimes fluid; give diuretics as prescribed and monitor potassium; watch for digoxin toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, bradycardia — check apical pulse and withhold if < 60/min per protocol).
k: Digoxin: check apical pulse; toxicity signs

notes.b: Chest pain suggestive of myocardial infarction (central, crushing, radiating to arm/jaw, with sweating) requires immediate ECG, oxygen if saturation low, aspirin (chewed) and nitrates as prescribed, analgesia (morphine), and continuous monitoring for arrhythmias. Anticoagulants: heparin (monitor aPTT for unfractionated heparin; antidote protamine) and warfarin (monitor INR; antidote vitamin K; avoid drug interactions and alcohol, keep dietary vitamin K consistent). Observe for bleeding (gums, urine, stools). Shock: position flat with legs raised (unless contraindicated), oxygen, IV access and fluids as prescribed, monitor vital signs and urine output.
k: MI: ECG, aspirin, nitrates, oxygen if hypoxic
